1:1.t: "East of the Jordan": the KJV's "on this side Jordan". The Hebrew be'ever hayyarden means "across the Jordan", here the east side, where Moses spoke.

1:5.t: "East of the Jordan": the KJV's "on this side Jordan". The Hebrew be'ever hayyarden means "across the Jordan", here the east side, where Moses spoke.

1:4.t: "In Ashtaroth and in Edrei": the KJV reads "at Astaroth in Edrei".

1:7.t: "Lowlands": the KJV's "the vale", the Shephelah, the foothills toward the coast.

1:28.t: Anakim, Emim, Zamzummim, Avvim, Caphtorim: the KJV adds an English -s (Anakims, Emims). The -im ending is already plural in Hebrew.

2:10.t: Anakim, Emim, Zamzummim, Avvim, Caphtorim: the KJV adds an English -s (Anakims, Emims). The -im ending is already plural in Hebrew.

2:21.t: Anakim, Emim, Zamzummim, Avvim, Caphtorim: the KJV adds an English -s (Anakims, Emims). The -im ending is already plural in Hebrew.

1:31.t: "As a father carries his son": the KJV's "as a man doth bear his son".
"Carried you": the image of God as a father carrying a child returns in Hosea 11:3 and Isaiah 46:3-4. Acts 13:18 echoes this verse in some Greek manuscripts.

1:41.t: "Thinking it easy": the KJV's "ye were ready". The Hebrew verb is rare.

2:8.t: "Arabah": the KJV's "the plain", the rift valley south of the Dead Sea. Ezion-geber: the KJV spells it Ezion-gaber.

2:23.t: "Gaza": the KJV's "Azzah". "Villages": the KJV takes Hazerim as a place name.

3:9.t: Senir: the KJV spells it Shenir.

3:10.t: "Plateau": the KJV's "the plain". Salecah: the KJV spells it Salchah.

3:11.t: KJV: "nine cubits ... four cubits, after the cubit of a man". "Bed": the Hebrew eres may also mean a coffin or sarcophagus.

3:14.t: "Havvoth-jair": the KJV's "Bashan-havoth-jair". It means "villages of Jair". Maacathites: the KJV's "Maachathi".

3:17.t: Kinnereth: the Sea of Galilee; the KJV spells it Chinnereth. "Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea": the Dead Sea.

4:20.t: "Iron-smelting furnace": the KJV's "iron furnace", a picture of Egypt as a place of fiery suffering and refining.

4:48.t: Mount Sion here is another name for Hermon, spelled differently in Hebrew from Zion in Jerusalem.

5:6.t: The Ten Commandments as given in Exodus 20:2-17, with small differences: the Sabbath command here rests on Israel's release from slavery (5:15) rather than on creation (Exodus 20:11), and the wife is listed before the house in 5:21. See the notes on Exodus 20.

6:8.t: "Bind them on your foreheads": the KJV's "as frontlets between thine eyes". See Exodus 13:9, 13:16.

6:9.t: Jewish homes keep this command with the mezuzah, a small case on the doorpost holding these verses.

7:6.t: "Treasured possession": the KJV's "special people". See Exodus 19:5.

7:26.t: "Set apart for destruction": the KJV's "a cursed thing", Hebrew cherem.

8:15.t: "Poisonous snakes": the KJV's "fiery serpents", named for their burning bite (Numbers 21:6).

9:2.t: "Anakim": the KJV's "children of the Anakims ... children of Anak".

10:6.t: "The wells of the Jaakanites": the KJV's "Beeroth of the children of Jaakan". Moserah, Jotbathah: the KJV spells them Mosera, Jotbath.

11:10.t: "Watered it by foot": irrigation in Egypt used foot-powered water wheels or channels opened with the foot. Canaan depended on rain.

11:14.t: "Early and late rains": the autumn rains that begin the growing season and the spring rains that finish it.

11:24.t: "Western sea": the KJV's "uttermost sea", the Mediterranean.

11:30.t: "Arabah": the KJV's "the champaign", meaning open country.

12:6.t: "Contributions of your hands": the KJV's "heave offerings of your hand". See Exodus 29:27-28.

12:11.t: "Contributions of your hands": the KJV's "heave offerings of your hand". See Exodus 29:27-28.

12:17.t: "Contributions of your hands": the KJV's "heave offerings of your hand". See Exodus 29:27-28.

12:15.t: "Gazelle or deer": the KJV's "roebuck ... hart", wild animals that could be eaten but not sacrificed.

12:22.t: "Gazelle or deer": the KJV's "roebuck ... hart", wild animals that could be eaten but not sacrificed.

13:6.t: "Your own full brother": the KJV's "thy brother, the son of thy mother".

13:16.t: "As a whole burnt offering": the KJV's "every whit, for the LORD thy God". The Hebrew kalil means a whole offering, completely burned.

14:1.t: "Shave the front of your heads": the KJV's "make any baldness between your eyes", a pagan mourning custom.
"You are the children of the LORD your God": Israel as God's son was first stated in Exodus 4:22. Their identity as His children is the reason for their distinct customs.

14:5.t: Several of these animals and birds cannot be identified with certainty; compare Leviticus 11:13-19. "Ibex": the KJV's "pygarg". "Mountain sheep": the KJV's "chamois".

14:12.t: Several of these animals and birds cannot be identified with certainty; compare Leviticus 11:13-19. "Ibex": the KJV's "pygarg". "Mountain sheep": the KJV's "chamois".

14:22.t: "Set aside a tenth": the KJV's "truly tithe". See Leviticus 27:30.

15:1.t: "Cancel debts": the KJV's "make a release". The Hebrew shemittah may mean cancelling the debt entirely or suspending payment for that year.

15:4.t: "There should be no poor among you": the KJV's "Save when there shall be no poor among you". Verse 11 recognizes the poor will always be present; verse 4 states the goal. Jesus echoes verse 11 in Mark 14:7.

16:3.t: "Bread of affliction": unleavened bread, made in haste, recalling the hardship of slavery and the rush of the exodus.

16:8.t: "Closing assembly": the KJV's "solemn assembly". See Leviticus 23:36.

16:13.t: "Festival of Booths": the KJV's "feast of tabernacles". See Leviticus 23:34.

16:21.t: "Asherah pole": the KJV's "a grove of any trees". 16:22 "Sacred pillar": the KJV's "image".

17:8.t: "Bloodshed, lawsuits, or assaults": the KJV's "between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke".

19:5.t: "The head may fly off the handle": the KJV's "the head slippeth from the helve". Some read it as a chip flying off the tree.

19:14.t: "Boundary stone": the KJV's "landmark". Moving it was a way of stealing land (Proverbs 22:28).

20:7.t: "Become engaged": the KJV's "betrothed". In Israel, betrothal was a binding agreement before the wedding.

20:19.t: "For is the tree of the field a man, that you should besiege it?": the KJV reads "for the tree of the field is man's life". The Hebrew can be read either way.

21:4.t: "A valley with a flowing stream": the KJV's "a rough valley". The Hebrew ethan can mean either.

21:15.t: "Unloved": the KJV's "hated". Hebrew uses "hated" for "loved less" (compare Genesis 29:30-31).

21:20.t: "Glutton and drunkard": Jesus' critics used these words against Him (Matthew 11:19).

22:8.t: "Railing": the KJV's "battlement". Flat roofs were used as living space.

22:9.t: "Forfeited to the sanctuary": the KJV's "defiled". The Hebrew verb qadash, "become holy", means the crop would belong to the sanctuary.

22:19.t: KJV: "an hundred shekels of silver"; "fifty shekels of silver".

22:29.t: KJV: "an hundred shekels of silver"; "fifty shekels of silver".

22:30.t: "Dishonor his father's bed": the KJV's "discover his father's skirt". In the Hebrew Bible this verse is 23:1, and the verses of chapter 23 are numbered one higher.

23:1.t: "Emasculated": the KJV's "wounded in the stones, or hath his privy member cut off". Isaiah 56:3-5 promises such people a place in God's house, and Acts 8:27-38 tells of an Ethiopian eunuch baptized.

23:13.t: "Something to dig with": the KJV's "a paddle upon thy weapon".

23:18.t: "Male prostitute": the KJV's "a dog", a term of contempt for a male cult prostitute.

24:6.t: "Livelihood": the KJV's "life". Taking a millstone took away the means to grind daily bread.

24:8.t: "Serious skin disease": the KJV's "leprosy". See Leviticus 13:2.

25:3.t: "Forty lashes": later Jewish practice gave thirty-nine to avoid exceeding the limit by mistake; Paul received this five times (2 Corinthians 11:24).

25:10.t: "The Family of the Unsandaled": the KJV's "The house of him that hath his shoe loosed". Ruth 4:7-8 records a related sandal custom.

25:13.t: "Weights and measures": the KJV's "divers weights ... divers measures". Merchants cheated by buying with a heavy weight and selling with a light one.

26:13.t: "Sacred portion": the KJV's "hallowed things", the tithe.

27:2.t: "Coat them with plaster": the KJV's "plaister them with plaister", so the law could be written on the surface.

27:4.t: "Coat them with plaster": the KJV's "plaister them with plaister", so the law could be written on the surface.

28:22.t: "Drought": the KJV's "the sword". The Hebrew consonants can be read as either word.

28:27.t: "Tumors": the KJV's "emerods". "Festering sores": the KJV's "the scab".

28:53.t: These terrible scenes were fulfilled in the sieges of Samaria (2 Kings 6:28-29) and Jerusalem (Lamentations 4:10).

28:57.t: "The afterbirth": the KJV's "her young one that cometh out from between her feet".

29:1.t: In the Hebrew Bible this verse is 28:69, and the verses of chapter 29 are numbered one lower.

29:18.t: "Bitter poison": the KJV's "gall and wormwood", bitter and poisonous plants. Hebrews 12:15 warns against a "root of bitterness".

29:19.t: "Disaster on the watered land as well as the dry": the KJV's "to add drunkenness to thirst". The Hebrew is a proverb whose meaning is uncertain; it may mean sweeping away everything, wet and dry alike.

29:23.t: Zeboiim: the KJV spells it Zeboim. See Genesis 14:2.

30:3.t: "Restore your fortunes": the KJV's "turn thy captivity". The Hebrew phrase shuv shevut can mean either.

31:10.t: "The year for canceling debts": the KJV's "the year of release". See 15:1-2.

32:5.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult; the KJV reads "their spot is not the spot of his children".

32:8.t: "According to the number of the sons of Israel": as in the KJV and the standard Hebrew text. A Dead Sea Scroll and the Greek Old Testament read "sons of God", meaning heavenly beings set over the nations.

32:10.t: "Apple of His eye": the pupil, the most protected part of the eye.

32:14.t: "Curds": the KJV's "butter". "The finest kernels of wheat": the KJV's "the fat of kidneys of wheat".

32:22.t: "The grave": the KJV's "the lowest hell"; Hebrew Sheol. See Genesis 37:35.

32:27.t: The KJV text adds a stray "hath done" at the end; it is the KJV margin's alternate rendering and is not translated.

32:36.t: "Slave or free": the KJV's "shut up, or left".

32:43.t: The Greek Old Testament and a Dead Sea Scroll have a longer form of this verse, including "Let all God's angels worship Him", which Hebrews 1:6 quotes.
"Make atonement for His land" (Hebrew kipper): the song ends with God cleansing His land and people. See Exodus 29:33.

32:44.t: Joshua: the KJV's "Hoshea", Joshua's earlier name (Numbers 13:16).

33:2.t: "Myriads of holy ones": the KJV's "ten thousands of saints". Jude 14 echoes this.

33:12.t: "Between His shoulders": possibly meaning on God's back, as a father carries a child, or among the hills of Benjamin where the temple later stood.

33:17.t: "Wild ox": the KJV's "unicorns". The Hebrew re'em is a wild ox, now extinct.

33:25.t: "Bolts of your gates": the KJV's "thy shoes". The Hebrew word is uncertain.

34:2.t: "Western sea": the KJV's "utmost sea", the Mediterranean.

34:5.t: Moses could not have written the account of his own death; Jewish tradition attributed these verses to Joshua.

2:30.t: "Made his spirit stubborn": see Exodus 4:21. As with Pharaoh, Sihon's refusal is his own, and God uses it for His purpose.

2:34.t: "Devoted them to destruction" (Hebrew charam): see Exodus 22:20 and Leviticus 27:28-29. The KJV's "utterly destroyed". In Deuteronomy the practice is limited to the Canaanite nations of the land (20:16-18) and is given as judgment on their sins (9:4-5, Genesis 15:16), not as a pattern for war in general. Nations outside the land were offered peace first (20:10-15).

4:2.t: "Do not add ... do not take away": the same warning appears at 12:32, Proverbs 30:6 and Revelation 22:18-19.

4:4.t: "Held fast" (Hebrew davaq): the KJV's "cleave", the verb used of a man "holding fast to his wife" (Genesis 2:24). It describes close, loyal attachment to God.

4:24.t: "A consuming fire, a jealous God": see Exodus 20:5. Hebrews 12:29 quotes the first phrase.

4:29.t: "With all your heart and with all your soul" (Hebrew bekhol levavekha uvekhol naphshekha): the heart (lev) in Hebrew is the center of thought and will; the soul (nephesh) is the whole living self (see Genesis 2:7). The phrase means with your whole being. It anticipates 6:5 and is echoed in Jeremiah 29:13.

4:35.t: "The LORD is God; there is no other besides Him": Deuteronomy's plainest statement that the LORD alone is God, not just the greatest of many. Isaiah repeats it (Isaiah 45:5-6).

4:39.t: "The LORD is God; there is no other besides Him": Deuteronomy's plainest statement that the LORD alone is God, not just the greatest of many. Isaiah repeats it (Isaiah 45:5-6).

4:37.t: "Loved ... chose" (Hebrew ahav ... bachar): God's choice of Israel rests only on His love, not on Israel's size or merit (7:7-8).

5:21.t: "Desire" (Hebrew chamad) ... "covet" (Hebrew hit'avveh): two verbs for wanting what is not yours. Exodus 20:17 uses chamad for both; here the second is a broader word for craving.

6:4.t: "The LORD our God, the LORD is one" (Hebrew shema yisra'el YHWH eloheinu YHWH echad): this is the Shema, named for its first word, "Hear". It is the center of Jewish prayer, recited morning and evening. The Hebrew can be read "The LORD our God, the LORD is one", "The LORD is our God, the LORD alone", or "The LORD our God is one LORD" (KJV). Echad means one, unique, or alone; the same word describes husband and wife becoming "one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). Jesus calls this and the next verse the greatest commandment (Mark 12:29-30).

6:5.t: "Love ... with all your heart, soul, and strength" (Hebrew ahav; lev, nephesh, me'od): love here is loyal, wholehearted devotion that shows itself in obedience (see 4:29 for heart and soul). Me'od usually means "very" or "much"; as a noun it means everything you have, your strength and resources. Jesus adds "mind" (Mark 12:30), drawing out what "heart" means in Hebrew.

6:7.t: "Teach them diligently" (Hebrew shinnantam): from shanan, "to sharpen". The words are to be impressed on children, cut in deeply, by repetition in all of life.

6:16.t: "Do not put the LORD your God to the test": see Exodus 17:2, 17:7. Jesus quotes this verse to Satan (Matthew 4:7), and 6:13 and 8:3 as well.

6:25.t: "Our righteousness" (Hebrew tsedaqah): here righteousness is right standing within the covenant, shown by faithful obedience. It is a response to God's saving act (6:21-23), not a way of earning it. See Genesis 15:6.

7:7.t: "Set His love on you" (Hebrew chashaq): a word for strong attachment or desire. God's love, not Israel's merit, is the only reason given for His choice.

7:9.t: "Covenant of steadfast love" (Hebrew habberit vehachesed): the KJV's "covenant and mercy". See Genesis 24:27 and Exodus 34:6-7.

8:3.t: "Man does not live on bread alone" (Hebrew lo al hallechem levaddo yichyeh ha'adam): "bread" stands for food in general and for everything people rely on to live. God's word is the deeper source of life. Jesus answers Satan's first temptation with this verse (Matthew 4:4).

8:5.t: "Disciplines" (Hebrew yasar): to train, correct and instruct, as a father raises a son, not only to punish. Proverbs 3:11-12 and Hebrews 12:5-11 build on this picture.

9:4.t: "Because of my righteousness": Moses rules out three times any idea that Israel earned the land. The two reasons given are the wickedness of the nations (Genesis 15:16) and God's faithfulness to His promise.

10:12.t: "What does the LORD your God ask of you": a summary of the covenant: fear, walk, love, serve, keep. Micah 6:8 echoes the form: "what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, to love steadfast love, and to walk humbly with your God?"

10:16.t: "Circumcise your hearts" (Hebrew umaltem et orlat levavkhem, "circumcise the foreskin of your heart"): outward circumcision was to be matched by an inward one, a heart opened to God. See Leviticus 26:41. In 30:6 God promises to do this Himself.

10:17.t: "God of gods and Lord of lords": a Hebrew way of saying the supreme God and supreme Lord. Revelation 17:14 and 19:16 give the title to Christ. "Shows no partiality" (lo yissa panim, "does not lift up faces"): He does not favor anyone because of status (Acts 10:34, Romans 2:11).

10:18.t: "Loves the foreigner ... you also must love the foreigner": see Leviticus 19:33-34. God's own character is the reason for Israel's care of the vulnerable.

12:5.t: "The place the LORD your God will choose ... to put His name there": this phrase appears about twenty times in Deuteronomy. The place is not named; it later proved to be Jerusalem (1 Kings 8:29, 2 Chronicles 6:6). God's "name" stands for His presence and character. Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when true worship will not depend on a place (John 4:21-24).

12:8.t: "Whatever is right in his own eyes": this phrase becomes the refrain of Judges, describing the chaos when everyone did as he pleased (Judges 17:6, 21:25).

12:23.t: "The blood is the life" (Hebrew haddam hu hannephesh): see Leviticus 17:11.

12:31.t: "Burn their sons and daughters": child sacrifice, the most detestable practice of Canaanite religion. See Leviticus 18:21.

13:3.t: "The LORD your God is testing you" (Hebrew nasah): even a sign that comes true is no proof of a true prophet if he leads people away from the LORD. Compare 18:22 and Matthew 24:24.

13:5.t: "Purge the evil from among you" (Hebrew uvi'arta hara miqqirbekha): a refrain in Deuteronomy (17:7, 19:19, 21:21, 22:21, 24:7). Paul quotes it about church discipline in 1 Corinthians 5:13.

13:13.t: "Worthless men" (Hebrew bene veliyya'al, "sons of Belial"): beliyya'al probably means "without worth". In later Jewish writing and in 2 Corinthians 6:15, Belial became a name for Satan.

15:7.t: "Hardhearted ... tightfisted ... openhanded" (Hebrew lo te'ammets et levavekha velo tiqpots et yadekha ... patoach tiftach et yadekha): the Hebrew pictures a hardened heart and a closed fist, against an open hand. 1 John 3:17 asks how God's love can be in anyone who closes his heart to a brother in need.

16:20.t: "Justice and justice alone" (Hebrew tsedeq tsedeq tirdof, "justice, justice you shall pursue"): the doubled word gives emphasis. Tsedeq means what is right, fair and true; "pursue" means chase after it actively.

17:6.t: "Two or three witnesses": the principle that no one may be condemned on one person's word. Jesus applies it to church discipline (Matthew 18:16), and Paul cites it (2 Corinthians 13:1, 1 Timothy 5:19).

17:14.t: The law of the king: Israel's king was to be under God's law, not above it. He was not to build power through horses (military might), many wives (foreign alliances and idolatry), or wealth. Solomon broke all three (1 Kings 10:26-11:4).

17:18.t: "A copy of this law" (Hebrew mishneh hattorah hazzot): the Greek Old Testament translated this as deuteronomion, "second law", which gave the book its English name, Deuteronomy. The Hebrew means a copy or repetition.

18:10.t: Forbidden practices: these terms cover several ways of trying to learn the future or control events apart from God: divination (qosem), interpreting omens (me'onen, menachesh), sorcery and spells (mekhashsheph, chover chaver), and contacting the dead (sho'el ov veyiddeoni, doresh el hammetim). King Saul later broke this command at Endor (1 Samuel 28).

18:15.t: "A Prophet like me" (Hebrew navi ... kamoni): the KJV capitalizes Prophet, following the long Christian reading of this promise as pointing to Christ, so the pronouns are capitalized here as well. In context it also promises a line of true prophets to speak for God, in contrast to the diviners of verses 10-14. In the New Testament, Peter and Stephen apply it directly to Jesus (Acts 3:22-23, 7:37), and the crowds ask John the Baptist whether he is "the Prophet" (John 1:21, 6:14).

18:18.t: "A Prophet like me" (Hebrew navi ... kamoni): the KJV capitalizes Prophet, following the long Christian reading of this promise as pointing to Christ, so the pronouns are capitalized here as well. In context it also promises a line of true prophets to speak for God, in contrast to the diviners of verses 10-14. In the New Testament, Peter and Stephen apply it directly to Jesus (Acts 3:22-23, 7:37), and the crowds ask John the Baptist whether he is "the Prophet" (John 1:21, 6:14).

19:6.t: "The avenger of blood" (Hebrew go'el haddam): the nearest relative responsible for avenging a murdered family member. The same word go'el means redeemer; see Exodus 6:6. The cities of refuge limited his vengeance to actual murderers.

19:21.t: "Life for life, eye for eye": see Exodus 21:23-25. Here the principle applies to a false witness, who receives the penalty he tried to bring on another.

20:16.t: "Do not leave alive anything that breathes": see the note on 2:34. Deuteronomy itself distinguishes these nearby Canaanite cities from distant cities, which were first offered peace (20:10-15).

21:23.t: "Anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse" (Hebrew qilelat elohim taluy): the body of an executed criminal was displayed on a pole as a sign of judgment. Paul quotes this verse of Christ: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). The Gospels note that Jesus' body was taken down before nightfall (John 19:31).

23:2.t: "Born of a forbidden union" (Hebrew mamzer): the KJV's "bastard". The exact meaning is uncertain. It probably refers to a child of incest or adultery, not simply a child born outside marriage. "Tenth generation" means permanently.

23:3.t: Ammonites and Moabites: yet Ruth the Moabite was welcomed into Israel and became David's great-grandmother (Ruth 4:13-22). Nehemiah 13:1-3 applies this verse in the time after the exile.

23:15.t: The escaped slave: unlike other ancient law codes, which demanded the return of runaway slaves, Israel was to shelter them. Compare Paul's letter to Philemon.

23:17.t: "Shrine prostitute" (Hebrew qedeshah, qadesh): from qadosh, "holy" or "set apart", a person who served in sexual rites at pagan shrines. The KJV's "sodomite" here translates qadesh. See Genesis 38:21.

24:1.t: "Something indecent" (Hebrew ervat davar, "nakedness of a thing"): the meaning was debated in Jesus' day. The school of Shammai limited it to sexual unfaithfulness; the school of Hillel allowed divorce for almost any reason. Jesus answers that Moses permitted divorce because of hard hearts, but God's purpose from creation was lifelong marriage (Matthew 19:3-9). The law here does not command divorce; it regulates it to protect the woman, who receives a written certificate so she is free to remarry.

24:16.t: "Each is to die for his own sin": individual responsibility before the law. Amaziah obeyed this verse (2 Kings 14:6), and Ezekiel 18 develops it.

25:4.t: "Do not muzzle an ox": the working animal must be allowed to eat from what it works. Paul applies the verse to support for those who preach the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:9-10, 1 Timothy 5:18).

25:5.t: "Fulfill the duty of a brother-in-law" (Hebrew yabbem): this is levirate marriage, from the Latin levir, "brother-in-law". It protected the widow and kept the dead man's name and land in his family. Compare Genesis 38 and Ruth 4. The Sadducees asked Jesus a question based on this law (Matthew 22:23-33).

26:5.t: "A wandering Aramean" (Hebrew arammi oved avi): the KJV reads "A Syrian ready to perish was my father". The verb avad can mean "perishing", "lost", or "wandering". The father is Jacob, who lived in Aram with Laban (Genesis 29-31). This confession, said each year with the firstfruits, sums up Israel's story: landless wanderer, slavery, deliverance, gift of the land.

26:17.t: "You have declared ... the LORD has declared" (Hebrew he'emarta ... he'emirkha): a rare verb, perhaps "caused to say", marking a solemn, two-sided covenant declaration: God is Israel's God, and Israel is God's people.

27:15.t: "Amen" (Hebrew amen): from aman, "to be firm" or "reliable", the same root as emet, "truth" (see Genesis 24:27), and he'emin, "to believe" (Genesis 15:6). Saying "Amen" means "It is true; so be it", binding oneself to what was said. Jesus begins many sayings with it, often translated "Truly" (see John 1).

27:26.t: "Cursed is anyone who does not uphold the words of this law": Paul quotes this verse to show that all who rely on keeping the law are under a curse, since no one keeps it fully, and that Christ took that curse (Galatians 3:10, 3:13).

28:1.t: Blessings and curses: ancient treaties often ended with blessings for loyalty and curses for betrayal. Here the covenant between God and Israel follows that pattern, with the curses described at greater length because Moses foresaw Israel's failure (31:16-21). Leviticus 26 has a parallel list.

28:63.t: "It pleased the LORD ... so it will please Him" (Hebrew sas): the boldness of the language stresses how certain and complete the judgment will be. Elsewhere God says, "I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezekiel 33:11), and 30:1-10 promises restoration.

28:68.t: "Back to Egypt": the reversal of the exodus. The people God freed from slavery would end up offering themselves as slaves, so worthless that no one would buy them.

29:4.t: "A mind that understands, or eyes that see, or ears that hear": Paul quotes this verse in Romans 11:8. Understanding God's works is His gift, not a human achievement; compare 30:6.

29:29.t: "The secret things belong to the LORD": what God has not revealed is His concern; what He has revealed is given for obedience. The verse sets a limit on speculation and a duty to obey.

30:2.t: "Return" (Hebrew shuv): to turn around, to repent. The same verb is used of God "restoring" Israel (30:3). This is the main Old Testament word for repentance; it means a change of direction, not only of feeling.

30:8.t: "Return" (Hebrew shuv): to turn around, to repent. The same verb is used of God "restoring" Israel (30:3). This is the main Old Testament word for repentance; it means a change of direction, not only of feeling.

30:10.t: "Return" (Hebrew shuv): to turn around, to repent. The same verb is used of God "restoring" Israel (30:3). This is the main Old Testament word for repentance; it means a change of direction, not only of feeling.

30:6.t: "Circumcise your hearts": see 10:16. There Israel is commanded to do it; here God promises to do it Himself. Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26 develop this promise of a new heart, and Paul speaks of "circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit" (Romans 2:29).

30:11.t: "The word is very near you": God's command is not remote or beyond human reach. Paul applies these verses to "the word of faith we proclaim": confessing with the mouth that Jesus is Lord and believing in the heart (Romans 10:6-10).

30:19.t: "Choose life": the covenant sets before Israel a real choice between life and death, blessing and curse. "Life" here means the full life of blessing in God's presence. Verse 20 identifies the source: "He is your life."

31:6.t: "He will never leave you nor forsake you" (Hebrew lo yarpekha velo ya'azvekka): Hebrews 13:5 quotes this promise and applies it to every believer.

31:8.t: "He will never leave you nor forsake you" (Hebrew lo yarpekha velo ya'azvekka): Hebrews 13:5 quotes this promise and applies it to every believer.

31:17.t: "Hide My face" (Hebrew hester panim): to withdraw favor and protection, the opposite of the priestly blessing, "The LORD make His face shine on you" (Numbers 6:25).

32:4.t: "The Rock" (Hebrew hatstsur): a title for God used five times in this song (32:4, 15, 18, 30, 31). A rock is firm, enduring and a place of refuge. Paul says the rock that gave Israel water "was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4).

32:15.t: "Jeshurun" (Hebrew yeshurun): a poetic name for Israel, probably from yashar, "upright". It is used with irony here: the "upright one" grew fat and rebelled.

32:17.t: "Demons" (Hebrew shedim): the KJV's "devils". Paul says sacrifices to idols are offered to demons (1 Corinthians 10:20).

32:21.t: "Those who are no people": Paul quotes this verse to explain how God uses the Gentiles to make Israel jealous (Romans 10:19, 11:11).

32:35.t: "It is Mine to avenge; I will repay": vengeance belongs to God, so His people are not to take it into their own hands. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 12:19, and Hebrews 10:30 as well.

32:39.t: "I, I am He" (Hebrew ani ani hu): an emphatic statement that the LORD alone is God. Isaiah takes up the phrase (Isaiah 41:4, 43:10, 43:25), and it may stand behind Jesus' "I am He" in John 8:24, 8:28, 13:19.

33:27.t: "The eternal God is your refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms": the Hebrew can also be read "The God of old is a dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms". Either way it pictures God as both a home above and a support beneath.

34:10.t: "Whom the LORD knew face to face": compare Exodus 33:11 and Numbers 12:8. This verse, written long after Moses, looks for the Prophet promised in 18:15-18. Hebrews 3:1-6 compares Moses, faithful as a servant in God's house, with Christ, faithful as a Son over it.
